So what happens after opens like this?  Outside of the Tech bust, it's been a long-term buying opportunity but more mixed short-term for the Nasdaq.

I looked at every S&P 500 open at least 2% above the prior close and every Nasdaq open at least 3% above (about 3 standard deviations each) since 2000. I counted only the first in any one-month cluster and measured from the close of the gap day.

Short term, the S&P has usually kept going. The Nasdaq has been choppier:

▪️ S&P 500 (32 cases): a week later it was higher 66% of the time (median +1.3%), and a month later 72% of the time (median +2.9%). For all days since 2000, those figures are 57% and 63% (median +0.3% and +1.2%).
▪️ Nasdaq since 2003 (11 cases): a week and a month later it was higher only 55% of the time (median +0.3% for both), below an average day. That includes one-month drops of 22% (September 2008), 9% (May 2010) and 7% (October 2008).

Longer term, both have done well:

▪️ S&P 500: median +9.5% six months later and +16.5% a year later, vs. +5.4% and +11.1% for all days.
▪️ Nasdaq since 2003: higher six months later in 10 of 11, with a median gain of +21.7% vs. +8.3% for all days.

The exception on the latter is the dot-com bust. Ten of the 21 Nasdaq cases since 2000 came in 2000–2002, when big gap-ups were mostly bear-market rallies that faded. Include them and the Nasdaq was higher a year later only 48% of the time.

Opens this big happen in stressed markets. Going into Monday, the Nasdaq was about 10% below its 200-day moving average, and 28 of the 32 S&P cases also came below that line. Outside 2000–2002, though, they've more often marked a low forming than a trap. The samples are small and 2020 and 2025 do a lot of the work, so keep that in mind.

While correlations had been increasing during the selloff, Xu says that changed Friday:

Friday’s move was about idiosyncratic risk, not macro: Single stock vol outpaced the increase in index vol on Friday, with the VIXEQSM Index jumping over 11 pts to a 1-year high of 58% (vs. VIX Index up 7pts). 

In other words, expected dispersion increased even as the market sold off almost 4%, as can be seen in the DSPXSM Index rising 5 pts on Friday (see Exhibit 3). 

This comes as investors rotate out of the AI theme into other sectors, rather than selling everything indiscriminately. As tech stocks fall out of favor, Tech vols have risen the most, with QQQ 1M implied vol jumping over 20 pts last week, the most of any global index. In contrast, US small cap volatility, which has very little exposure to the AI theme, saw its volatility trail that of its large-cap counterparts. The RTY-SPX 1M implied vol spread narrowed to a 6-year low of 1.4% as a result.

CBOE's Mandy Xu: Friday’s VIX move, while large, was  surprisingly orderly. The sell-off in SPX® spot (-3.7%) and the  increase in fixed-strike vols (+3.2 pts) accounted for almost  90% of the 7.4pt VIX increase. 

Very little came from demand for downside puts. In fact, changes in skew and convexity contributed just 0.9pt to the VIX move (see Exhibit 2). In contrast, demand for downside protection made up almost half of the Nov 5th VIX spike. This can also be seen in  measures of SPX 1M skew (25-delta ratio), which spiked to  the 95th percentile high after the Nov 5th sell-off but only  steepened modestly to the 80th percentile last Friday. 

Also  notable was the lack of demand for upside calls on Friday, with call skew falling and call convexity unchanged. It seems that while there was little panic on Friday, investors were also not positioning for a quick rebound.

@C_Barraud's Morning Brief is packed with posts about the equity selloff (along with a lot of other stuff) including @MikeZaccardi's post that Goldman's US Financial Conditions Index excluding equities hit a new cycle high, "along with intensely bearish Fed speak."

That fits with the analysis I ran in the Week Ahead:
▪ Goldman's headline FCI tightened 46bp last week to 99.53, the biggest weekly tightening since March 2020 and the ninth-largest since 1990, leaving it the tightest since April 2025.
▪ Stocks did most of it (about 35bp from Monday's close through Friday), with, with credit spreads and the dollar adding about 5bp each and lower long-term yields offsetting about 9bp.
▪ The ex-equities line shows conditions outside of stocks were already tight. Goldman says the two series "diverged" over the past few years, but "both series have tightened in recent months."
▪ The Fed's own FCI-G said the same thing in October: stocks supplied 96% of what was left of the tailwind to growth, everything else netted to about zero, and interest rates had turned into a drag.
▪ But the Fed isn't backing off. By my count all 16 of the 19 FOMC participants who have spoken on rates since the November 5 selloff have signaled more tightening, and Philadelphia's Paulson, one of the most dovish members, said Friday she'd be open to considering back-to-back hikes.

So we've clearly not gotten to the point of a "Fed put," but with the biggest accommodative factor quickly losing steam, the words "policy mistake" are being uttered more and more. 

One silver lining: after the 12 prior weeks since 1990 when Goldman's FCI tightened 41bp or more, the S&P 500 was higher three months later 11 times (median +6.5%, about double normal), though the first week was a coin flip and October 2008 was the big exception.

Since 2017 (TradingView's Nasdaq volume data for 2015–16 run far below other years, so I started after that), there have been 24 prior readings of Nasdaq positive volume below 20%, counting only the first in any 21 sessions. 

The Nasdaq was higher a week later 75% of the time (median +1.3%, vs. 60% and +0.6% for all days). From a month out, though, the results were about in line with all days, and a year later its median gain (13.1%) trailed the all-days figure (21.9%), although it was higher about as often (83% vs. 84%).

Unlike on the NYSE, readings that came with the Nasdaq already 10% or more below its record, as it is now (18.1% below at Friday's close), did worse, with a median 1.4% loss a month later and the index higher only three of seven times. 

Four of those seven came during the 2022 bear market, though. The two most recent, April 4, 2025 and March 27, 2026, were followed by one-month gains of 13.5% and 17.7%.
